Here, we'll introduce the last variant of ANOVA that we'll deal with: the factorial ANOVA, meaning ANOVA used with research designs that have more than one independent variable. This enables us to see not just the effect of a single variable, but how two variables interact. It's slightly more complicated, both conceptually and mathematically, but it's based on the same idea of partitioning variance that we've used in the previous two chapters.

## Factorial designs

<!-- CUT (terminology recap, Chapter 14 covers factor and levels; plan §4.1). Kept verbatim.

To refresh your memory of the terminology that goes with the ANOVA procedure, a factor means the variable that defines the different groups being compared, usually an independent variable that the researcher manipulates either between or within participants — like our examples where we gave people different snacks before a test. Snack type was the factor there. The levels are the individual conditions that make up a factor. So we have different groups for the banana, the candy bar, and the control condition. Those were the levels of the snack factor.
-->

A factorial design, then, is one with more than one factor, each factor with two or more levels. For our purposes, we're only going to look at one kind of factorial design: the two-by-two between-participants ANOVA, which has two between-participants factors, each with two levels. But you should be aware that one or both factors can be manipulated within participants. And we can have more factors, and factors that have different numbers of levels — like we could have a three-by-two within-participants design. We can even have a mix of between- and within-participants factors. We call that a mixed-factorial design. But again, here we'll just stick with the two-by-two between-participants version.

### Structure of a two-by-two design

It's important to understand the basic conceptual structure here. With a two-by-two design, we end up with four actual samples, one for each combination of the levels of each factor. So generically, we have Factor A and Factor B. If we arrange them in a table, you can see the four conditions that that creates.

|  |  | **Factor A** | |
|---|---|:--:|:--:|
| | | $A_1$ | $A_2$ |
| **Factor B** | $B_1$ | $A_1 B_1$ | $A_2 B_1$ |
| | $B_2$ | $A_1 B_2$ | $A_2 B_2$ |

: The four conditions of a generic 2×2 factorial design. {#tbl-factorial-generic}

If you're a participant in this study, you might be in the group of people treated with level one of Factor A and level one of Factor B. Or you might get level one of Factor A and level two of Factor B. Or you could be in level two of Factor A, level one of Factor B. Or $A_2 B_2$.

<!-- FIX: check the "at least 30 participants per condition" claim against what Chapter 7 now says about the normality rule. -->

We can always find the number of individual groups by multiplying the factorial statement. So two-by-two literally means two multiplied by two, so four conditions in total. A two-by-three design would have two times three, so six groups. A three-by-five design would have three times five, so fifteen conditions. It can get pretty complicated. And you'd need a lot of participants because usually you'd want at least 30 participants per condition for the central limit theorem normality rule to kick in. But again, we'll just stick with a two-by-two design.

## Main effects and interactions

<!-- FIX: "each of the four conditions compared to each of the others" is wrong: in a 2×2 the interaction is a single difference of differences. -->

When it comes to the hypothesis test for a factorial design, we'll actually run several hypothesis tests. For this two-by-two design we'll have three tests. First, the main effects. We test the main effect of Factor A — this asks whether there is an overall difference between the levels of Factor A ignoring the levels of Factor B. We just pool everyone together depending on which level of Factor A they were in, regardless of their level of Factor B. Second, there's the main effect of Factor B. This is the same idea. We ignore the different groups on Factor A and just pool together everyone on each level of Factor B, and compare those two levels to see if there was an overall difference.

And third, we're interested in the interaction between A and B. This is the whole reason for coming up with a complicated design like this in the first place, instead of just two separate studies to look at Factors A and B in isolation. We want to know if Factor A and Factor B interact — that is, if the effect of one depends on the level of the other. So for this interaction test we'll look at each of the four conditions compared to each of the others, checking to see if that pattern of variability deviates from what we'd expect based on the main effects alone.

### Grouping scores for analysis

Again, when we come to analyze the data, we'll be grouping up the scores in different ways to analyze the different patterns of variability. For the main effect of maze difficulty, we'll be comparing everyone who did the easy maze against everyone who did the hard maze. And then for the main effect of Factor B, we compare everyone who worked alone with everyone who was watched. For the interaction, we're basically looking at the variability among all four cells of the table to see if anything departs from what we'd expect based on those main effects alone.

<!-- PLAN (2026-11-11): "Reading interaction graphs" used to sit here. Rob moved it to follow the worked analysis: it's now the tutorial in "Interpreting the results". The paragraph below opened that section and still works as the lead-in to the equations; check the join. -->

Before we get to the equations, a word about priorities: I'm much less interested in having you memorize all those different variations of variance equations than in making sure you understand the logic of factorial ANOVA on a more conceptual level and that you're able to interpret the pattern of findings that you might see.

## Partitioning variance

<!-- FIX: "chance variability" and "the variance expected if there is no treatment effect" should match Chapter 14's two-estimates wording. Each effect in a 2×2 has df = 1, so each F is a squared t, which is a one-line callback to Chapter 14 worth making. -->

So for each of those three hypotheses, we calculate an $F$ ratio. Though the math will differ slightly, because we'll be partitioning variance differently, the $F$ ratios all follow the same conceptual structure. We're comparing the variance between groups to the variance expected if there is no treatment effect. This should sound familiar. It's the same logic of the $t$ test and the other ANOVAs we've learned. But there's really nothing new here, just a more nuanced application of the basic concepts.

Calculating the various components required for those three $F$ ratios works just like any other ANOVA. Conceptually, we're partitioning the total variance in the data into different sources, just as before. It starts out the same as every other ANOVA. We separate the total variability into variability between groups and variability within groups, each measured by its sum of squares. Here each cell of the table is a group, so our 2×2 design has four groups.

Now here, assuming we're just using between-participants factors, we don't need to divide up the variance within groups. Instead, we want to think about the different sources of between-groups variability. We want to separate between-groups variability associated with Factor A exclusively and between-groups variability associated with Factor B exclusively. And knowing both of those, anything left over — any between-groups variability not accounted for by those main effects of Factor A and Factor B — must be due to the interaction between Factors A and B.

::: {#fig-partitioning-factorial}
{{< interactive-figure factorialPartitionDiagram makeVariancePartitionDiagram options='{"preset":"factorial","formula":false,"ariaLabel":"Diagram partitioning the total sum of squares into variability between groups, which contains treatment effects and chance, and variability within groups, which contains chance. The between-groups variability is further partitioned into Factor A, Factor B, and the A-by-B interaction, each containing its own main effect or interaction plus chance."}' fallback="Diagram partitioning the total sum of squares into variability between groups, which contains treatment effects and chance, and variability within groups, which contains chance. The between-groups variability is further partitioned into Factor A, Factor B, and the A-by-B interaction, each containing its own main effect or interaction plus chance." >}}
:::

Each component gets its own $F$ ratio, always compared against the same denominator: the mean square within groups, our estimate of chance variability. As always, we get each mean square by dividing a sum of squares by its degrees of freedom.

$$
\begin{aligned}
F_A &= \frac{MS_A}{MS_{\text{within}}} \\[1.5ex]
F_B &= \frac{MS_B}{MS_{\text{within}}} \\[1.5ex]
F_{A \times B} &= \frac{MS_{A \times B}}{MS_{\text{within}}}
\end{aligned}
$$

## Sums of squares and degrees of freedom

<!-- DRAFT (2026-11-09, written at Rob's request): this section now uses definitional formulas, as Chapters 14 and 15 do (ISSUES #5). The familiar three are restated without comment; the new ones are tied to the steps of act-factorial-anova-viz. Rob's sentences are kept where they still apply. Column and row symbols follow his "columns and rows" wording. The previous version is in the CUT comment at the end of the section. -->

So in terms of calculating these different components, it's the same basic process as before. First, we need to know various sums of squares and degrees of freedom. As always, we start with between and within groups $SS$ and $df$. And, again, now it's the between-groups variability that we further subdivide into the $SS$ and $df$ for Factor A, Factor B, and the remainder, which must be accounted for by the interaction.

The equations for the total, within-groups, and between-groups $SS$ and $df$ are exactly the same as in Chapter 14. Just remember that each cell of the table is a group, so here $k = 4$.

$$
\begin{align}
SS_{\text{total}} &= \Sigma (X - M_{\text{grand}})^2 \\
SS_{\text{within}} &= \Sigma (X - M_{\text{group}})^2 \\
SS_{\text{between}} &= \Sigma n_{\text{group}}(M_{\text{group}} - M_{\text{grand}})^2
\end{align}
$$

$$
\begin{align}
df_{\text{total}} &= N - 1 \\
df_{\text{within}} &= N - k \\
df_{\text{between}} &= k - 1
\end{align}
$$

The new equations[^factorial-computational] here are for the main effects and interaction.[^factorial-equal-n] And as long as we're thinking about the data in a two-by-two table like @tbl-factorial-generic, then we can think in terms of columns and rows.

[^factorial-computational]: As in Chapters 14 and 15, there are computational versions of these formulas. They use column totals and row totals in the same way that Chapter 14's used treatment totals. We'll stick with the definitional formulas here too.

[^factorial-equal-n]: These formulas assume that every group has the same number of scores. With unequal group sizes, the pieces no longer add up so neatly, and the analysis gets more complicated.

### Sums of squares for Factor A

In my generic table, I had Factor A at the top of the table, so its two conditions were represented as columns in the table. In @act-factorial-anova-viz, this was the part where we regrouped the scores by maze, ignoring the audience. We find the mean of all the scores in each column, $M_{\text{column}}$, and see how far it falls from the grand mean. Then we square that deviation and multiply it by $n_{\text{column}}$, the number of scores in the column, since each column mean represents that many scores.

$$ SS_A = \Sigma n_{\text{column}}(M_{\text{column}} - M_{\text{grand}})^2 $$

Notice that this is basically the same equation as for the between-groups sum of squares. The difference is that the means represent different sets of scores — scores for each column combined, rather than all four groups separately. It's the same move we made in Chapter 15 when we regrouped the scores by person. And its degrees of freedom are $k_A$, the number of levels for that factor, minus one.

$$ df_A = k_A - 1 $$

### Sums of squares for Factor B

And it's the same logic for the $SS$ for Factor B. In my generic table, Factor B was on the side of the table, so its two conditions were represented as rows. Now we regroup the scores by audience, ignoring the maze. Again, the only new thing about this equation is that the means represent another grouping of scores, the scores for each row combined, and the number of scores in each row.

$$ SS_B = \Sigma n_{\text{row}}(M_{\text{row}} - M_{\text{grand}})^2 $$

$$ df_B = k_B - 1 $$

### The interaction

And then, like I said, the $SS$ and $df$ for the interaction are simply whatever is left over — between-groups variability not already partitioned either into Factor A or Factor B. So we can find those through simple subtraction.

$$
\begin{align}
SS_{A \times B} &= SS_{\text{between}} - SS_A - SS_B \\
df_{A \times B} &= df_{\text{between}} - df_A - df_B
\end{align}
$$

For a two-by-two design, that leaves $3 - 1 - 1 = 1$ degree of freedom. More generally, it works out to $(k_A - 1)(k_B - 1)$, much like the error degrees of freedom in Chapter 15.

But, as with the error component in Chapter 15, we can also get the interaction directly from the data, which helps show what it represents. In @act-factorial-anova-viz, each group got a prediction: the mean we'd expect for that group if the two main effects were all that was going on. To make the prediction, we start at the grand mean, then adjust for how far the group's column mean is from the grand mean, and again for its row mean. That simplifies to $M_{\text{column}} + M_{\text{row}} - M_{\text{grand}}$.

The interaction is about how far each group's actual mean falls from that prediction. We square each of those differences and multiply by the number of scores in the group, just as we did for the between-groups sum of squares.

$$
\begin{aligned}
SS_{A \times B} = \Sigma n_{\text{group}}(&M_{\text{group}} - M_{\text{column}} \\
&{}- M_{\text{row}} + M_{\text{grand}})^2
\end{aligned}
$$

If there were no interaction at all, every group mean would sit right on its prediction, and this would come to zero. The farther the group means are from where the main effects alone would put them, the bigger the interaction.

### One equation, four groupings

Over the last three chapters we've now used what is basically the same equation four times: group the scores, find each group's mean, and see how far those means fall from the grand mean. All that changed was the grouping. @tbl-anova-groupings lines them up, much like the table comparing the $t$ statistics in Chapter 13.

| Component | Scores grouped by | Sum of squares |
|:--|:--|:--|
| Between groups (Ch. 14--16) | Condition, or cell | $\Sigma n_{\text{group}}(M_{\text{group}} - M_{\text{grand}})^2$ |
| Between people (Ch. 15) | Person | $\Sigma k(M_{\text{person}} - M_{\text{grand}})^2$ |
| Factor A (Ch. 16) | Column | $\Sigma n_{\text{column}}(M_{\text{column}} - M_{\text{grand}})^2$ |
| Factor B (Ch. 16) | Row | $\Sigma n_{\text{row}}(M_{\text{row}} - M_{\text{grand}})^2$ |

: The same equation with the scores grouped four different ways. In each case, the squared deviation of a mean from the grand mean is multiplied by the number of scores that mean represents. {#tbl-anova-groupings}

The two new components that aren't in the table, Chapter 15's error and this chapter's interaction, came from the other move we keep making: subtracting, to see what's left of a larger component once these have been taken out.

<!-- CUT (the computational-formula version of this section, replaced 2026-11-09). Kept verbatim.

So in terms of calculating these different components, it's the same basic process as before. First, we need to know various sums of squares and degrees of freedom. As always, we start with between and within groups $SS$ and $df$. And, again, now it's the between-groups variability that we further subdivide into the $SS$ and $df$ for Factor A, Factor B, and the remainder, which must be accounted for by the interaction.

So the equations for between and within groups $SS$ and $df$ are exactly the same as before. The new equations here are for the main effects and interaction. And as long as we're thinking about the data in a two-by-two table like I've shown you, then we can think in terms of columns and rows.

### Sums of squares for Factor A

In my generic table, I had Factor A at the top of the table, so its two conditions were represented as columns in the table. So the $SS$ for Factor A are the sum of $T^2_{\text{column}}$ divided by $n_{\text{column}}$, meaning the sum of scores for each column divided by the number of scores in each column, minus $G^2$ divided by $N$. Notice that this is basically the same equation as for the between-groups variance. The difference is that the $T$ represents different sets of scores — scores for each column combined, rather than all four treatment conditions separately. And its degrees of freedom are $k_A$, the number of levels for that factor, minus one.

### Sums of squares for Factor B

And it's the same logic for the $SS$ for Factor B. In my generic table, Factor B was on the side of the table, so its two conditions were represented as rows. So $SS$ for Factor B are the sum of $T^2_{\text{row}}$ divided by $n_{\text{row}}$ minus $G^2$ over $N$. Here we sum the scores for each row and we divide by the number of scores in each row. Again, the only new thing about this equation is that the $T$ scores represent another grouping of scores, the scores for each row combined, and the number of scores in each row.

### The interaction

And then, like I said, the $SS$ and $df$ for the interaction are simply whatever is left over — variability not already partitioned either into Factor A or Factor B. So we find those through simple subtraction.
-->

## A factorial ANOVA, step by step

So now let's work through a hypothesis test for this design, using the maze and audience example in @tbl-factorial-data. Each cell had just four recorded scores.

### Step 1: State the hypotheses

As always, we start with our hypotheses, and we have both a null hypothesis and alternative hypothesis for each of the three tests we're going to do: the main effect of maze difficulty, the main effect of audience, and the interaction. For the main effects, the null hypothesis is just that each level of the factor is equal to the other. The alternative hypothesis is that the levels are not equal to one another. For the interaction, our null hypothesis is that there is no interaction. The alternative is that there is.

<!-- DRAFT (gap): once the difference of differences is in place, the interaction null can be stated with it: the effect of being watched is the same on both mazes. The three hypotheses could also be written in symbols, as in Chapters 14 and 15. -->

### Step 2: Set the decision criteria

<!-- DRAFT (gap): Step 2 never gives the numbers. Each numerator has $df = 1$ (two levels minus one; the interaction's is what's left of $df_{\text{between}} = 3$), and $df_{\text{within}} = N - k = 16 - 4 = 12$, so the critical value for all three tests is 4.75.
     FIX: we're running three tests at .05 each, one chapter after Chapter 14's experiment-wise error rate. A reader may ask; a sentence on the convention would cover it. -->

Step two is to determine the critical value for the test. And we do so using the same $F$ table as before. Strictly speaking, we need three different critical values, one for each of our three hypothesis tests. But here with a two-by-two between-participants design, all three $F$ ratios actually have the same degrees of freedom, both for the numerator and the denominator. That won't always necessarily be the case. The denominator is always the same for all three tests, but the degrees of freedom for the numerator may vary if we have a more complicated design.

::: {#tbl-factorial-critical}
{{< interactive-figure factorialCriticalTable makeFTable options='{"title":"Critical values for the maze tests","alpha":0.05,"df1":{"from":1,"to":4},"df2":{"from":10,"to":14},"tableMinWidth":"0","maxWidth":"32rem","interactive":false,"selected":{"df1":1,"df2":12,"alpha":0.05}}' fallback="F table excerpt for numerator df 1 through 4 and denominator df 10 through 14, highlighting the .05 critical value of 4.75 at F(1, 12)." >}}

An excerpt of the $F$ table, with the critical value for $df = 1$ and $12$ highlighted.
:::

### Step 3: Collect and analyze the data

<!-- DRAFT (2026-11-09, written at Rob's request): Step 3 is now a definitional worked example, laid out like Chapter 15's. The paragraph introducing the means table is adapted from the one in the CUT comment below. The practice quiz at the end of the step uses separate numbers. -->

Again, there are a lot of values to keep track of while you calculate this, so filling in a summary table as you go is a good idea. Notice the new rows here for Factor A and Factor B and the interaction.

::: {#tbl-factorial-summary-blank .sfs-summary-table}
| Source | $SS$ | $df$ | $MS$ | $F$ |
|:-------|:--:|:--:|:--:|:--:|
| Between groups | $\Sigma n_{\text{group}}(M_{\text{group}} - M_{\text{grand}})^2$ | $k - 1$ | []{.sfs-na} | []{.sfs-na} |
| &emsp;Factor A | $\Sigma n_{\text{column}}(M_{\text{column}} - M_{\text{grand}})^2$ | $k_A - 1$ | $\dfrac{SS_A}{df_A}$ | $\dfrac{MS_A}{MS_{\text{within}}}$ |
| &emsp;Factor B | $\Sigma n_{\text{row}}(M_{\text{row}} - M_{\text{grand}})^2$ | $k_B - 1$ | $\dfrac{SS_B}{df_B}$ | $\dfrac{MS_B}{MS_{\text{within}}}$ |
| &emsp;A × B interaction | $SS_{\text{between}} - SS_A - SS_B$ | $df_{\text{between}} - df_A - df_B$ | $\dfrac{SS_{A \times B}}{df_{A \times B}}$ | $\dfrac{MS_{A \times B}}{MS_{\text{within}}}$ |
| Within groups | $\Sigma (X - M_{\text{group}})^2$ | $N - k$ | $\dfrac{SS_{\text{within}}}{df_{\text{within}}}$ | []{.sfs-na} |
| Total | $\Sigma (X - M_{\text{grand}})^2$ | $N - 1$ | []{.sfs-na} | []{.sfs-na} |

A factorial ANOVA summary table, showing each equation.
:::

So the $SS$ column has each of the sums of squares equations, the $df$ column has how to find each degrees of freedom value, and so on.

Step three is to calculate the test statistics. Here's the data table again. But like I've done before, I'm gonna give you some of the quantities you'll need to save you some time. Step three is to calculate the test statistics. Here's the data table again. But like I've done before, I'm going to give you some of the quantities you'll need to save you some time. So I've replaced the four scores in each cell with the group's mean and its sum of squared deviations. I've also added the mean of each row and each column, and the grand mean. And below, I'm giving you $N$, the total number of scores, lowercase $n$, the number in each group, $k$, the total number of groups, and $k_A$ and $k_B$, the number of levels for each factor.

|  | Easy maze | Hard maze | Row mean |
|:--|:--:|:--:|:--:|
| Alone | $M = 36$; $SS = 66$ | $M = 40$; $SS = 62$ | 38 |
| Watched | $M = 28$; $SS = 74$ | $M = 56$; $SS = 86$ | 42 |
| Column mean | 32 | 48 | $M_{\text{grand}} = 40$ |

: Means and sums of squares for each cell, with the row and column means. {#tbl-factorial-means}

$$
\begin{gathered}
N = 16 \qquad n = 4 \qquad k = 4 \\
k_A = 2 \qquad k_B = 2
\end{gathered}
$$

So see if you can calculate all the pieces of the puzzle and end up with three $F$ ratios for the main effects and the interaction.

Here's how it works out. First, the familiar components. For within groups, we can just add the four groups' sums of squares from @tbl-factorial-means:

$$
\begin{aligned}
SS_{\text{within}} &= \Sigma (X - M_{\text{group}})^2 \\
&= 66 + 62 + 74 + 86 \\
&= 288
\end{aligned}
$$

$$ df_{\text{within}} = N - k = 16 - 4 = 12 $$

For between groups, we find each group mean's deviation from the grand mean, square it, and multiply by the four scores it represents:

$$
\begin{aligned}
SS_{\text{between}} &= \Sigma n_{\text{group}}(M_{\text{group}} - M_{\text{grand}})^2 \\
&= 4(-4)^2 + 4(0)^2 \\
&\quad {}+ 4(-12)^2 + 4(16)^2 \\
&= 1{,}664
\end{aligned}
$$

$$ df_{\text{between}} = k - 1 = 4 - 1 = 3 $$

Those two add up to the total: $SS_{\text{total}} = 1{,}664 + 288 = 1{,}952$, with $df_{\text{total}} = N - 1 = 15$.

Now for the new components. For the maze factor, we use the column means, 32 and 48 seconds. Each one represents eight scores:

$$
\begin{aligned}
SS_A &= \Sigma n_{\text{column}}(M_{\text{column}} - M_{\text{grand}})^2 \\
&= 8(32 - 40)^2 + 8(48 - 40)^2 \\
&= 1{,}024
\end{aligned}
$$

$$ df_A = k_A - 1 = 2 - 1 = 1 $$

For the audience factor, we do the same with the row means, 38 and 42 seconds:

$$
\begin{aligned}
SS_B &= \Sigma n_{\text{row}}(M_{\text{row}} - M_{\text{grand}})^2 \\
&= 8(38 - 40)^2 + 8(42 - 40)^2 \\
&= 64
\end{aligned}
$$

$$ df_B = k_B - 1 = 2 - 1 = 1 $$

Then we can find the interaction by subtracting both of those from the between-groups component:

$$
\begin{aligned}
SS_{A \times B} &= SS_{\text{between}} - SS_A - SS_B \\
&= 1{,}664 - 1{,}024 - 64 \\
&= 576
\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}
df_{A \times B} &= df_{\text{between}} - df_A - df_B \\
&= 3 - 1 - 1 = 1
\end{aligned}
$$

But let's also see how the interaction builds up from the group means. Take the kids who did the easy maze alone. Their column mean is 32 and their row mean is 38, so the prediction is $32 + 38 - 40 = 30$ seconds. Their actual mean was 36 seconds: 6 seconds slower than the main effects alone would suggest. @tbl-factorial-predictions does the same for all four groups.

| Group | $M_{\text{group}}$ | Prediction | Difference |
|:--|--:|--:|--:|
| Easy, alone | 36 | $32 + 38 - 40 = 30$ | $6$ |
| Hard, alone | 40 | $48 + 38 - 40 = 46$ | $-6$ |
| Easy, watched | 28 | $32 + 42 - 40 = 34$ | $-6$ |
| Hard, watched | 56 | $48 + 42 - 40 = 50$ | $6$ |

: Each group's mean, the mean predicted from the two main effects alone, and the difference between them. {#tbl-factorial-predictions}

Every group mean is 6 seconds from its prediction, in one direction or the other. (That's always how it goes with a two-by-two design: the four differences come out the same size.) Squaring each difference and multiplying by the four scores in each group gives the same answer as before:

$$
\begin{aligned}
SS_{A \times B} &= 4(6)^2 + 4(-6)^2 \\
&\quad {}+ 4(-6)^2 + 4(6)^2 \\
&= 576
\end{aligned}
$$

Now we have all the sums of squares and their degrees of freedom. Dividing each one by its degrees of freedom gives the mean squares:

$$
\begin{align}
MS_A &= \frac{SS_A}{df_A} = \frac{1{,}024}{1} = 1{,}024 \\
MS_B &= \frac{SS_B}{df_B} = \frac{64}{1} = 64 \\
MS_{A \times B} &= \frac{SS_{A \times B}}{df_{A \times B}} = \frac{576}{1} = 576 \\
MS_{\text{within}} &= \frac{SS_{\text{within}}}{df_{\text{within}}} = \frac{288}{12} = 24
\end{align}
$$

Finally, we divide each of the three new mean squares by the within-groups mean square:

$$
\begin{align}
F_A &= \frac{MS_A}{MS_{\text{within}}} = \frac{1{,}024}{24} \approx 42.67 \\
F_B &= \frac{MS_B}{MS_{\text{within}}} = \frac{64}{24} \approx 2.67 \\
F_{A \times B} &= \frac{MS_{A \times B}}{MS_{\text{within}}} = \frac{576}{24} = 24.00
\end{align}
$$

Here's the completed summary table so you can check your work:

::: {#tbl-factorial-summary .sfs-summary-table}
| Source | $SS$ | $df$ | $MS$ | $F$ |
|:-------|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| Between groups | 1,664 | 3 | []{.sfs-na} | []{.sfs-na} |
| &emsp;Maze (A) | 1,024 | 1 | 1,024 | 42.67 |
| &emsp;Audience (B) | 64 | 1 | 64 | 2.67 |
| &emsp;A × B interaction | 576 | 1 | 576 | 24.00 |
| Within groups | 288 | 12 | 24 | []{.sfs-na} |
| Total | 1,952 | 15 | []{.sfs-na} | []{.sfs-na} |

Completed factorial ANOVA summary table for the maze × audience example.
:::

That's an impressive feat. It's the most mathematically complicated thing that we'll do in this book. It's worth working through the math by hand at least once to reinforce how this kind of ANOVA works behind the scenes.

{{< include quizzes/16-factorial-anova-calculate-2x2.qmd >}}

### Step 4: Make a decision

<!-- FIX: "there was no difference between the two test conditions" is accept-the-null language that Chapters 8-13 avoid. "Main effects don't mean too much" overstates; it depends on whether the interaction reverses the effect or only changes its size. -->

Here you should have found that the $F$ ratio was within the critical region for the main effect of maze difficulty (the critical value for $F(1, 12)$ at $\alpha = .05$ is 4.75). It was outside the critical region for audience. And within the critical region for the interaction.

<!-- FIGURE (2026-11-09): new, modeled on Chapter 14's fig-anova-decision, with all three Fs on one curve. Fine on desktop; on a phone the Audience and 4.75 labels sit close together at the left edge. Shorter labels or a narrower x-axis would help if it stays. -->

::: {#fig-factorial-decision}
{{< interactive-figure factorialTestDecision makeDistributionGraph options='{"color":"var(--sfs-null-color, currentColor)","distribution":"f","df1":1,"df2":12,"title":"Null distribution: F(1, 12)","style":"minimal","xAxis":true,"yLabel":false,"xDomain":[0,45],"yDomain":[0,1],"clipPlot":true,"xTicks":6,"labels":{"x":"F ratio"},"shade":{"tail":"right","alpha":0.05},"markers":[{"at":4.747225,"label":"4.75","height":0.45,"color":"var(--sfs-critical-color, #c63f3f)"},{"at":2.666667,"label":"Audience","height":0.75,"color":"var(--sfs-accent, #2c7fb8)"},{"at":24,"label":"Interaction","height":0.6,"color":"var(--sfs-accent, #2c7fb8)"},{"at":42.666667,"label":"Maze","height":0.6,"color":"var(--sfs-accent, #2c7fb8)"}],"maxWidth":"42rem"}' fallback="Null F distribution with 1 and 12 degrees of freedom. The rejection region lies above 4.75. The observed F for audience, 2.67, falls short of it; the observed Fs for the interaction, 24.00, and for maze, 42.67, are far into the rejection region." >}}

The three observed $F$ ratios against the null $F$ distribution with $df = 1$ and $12$. Audience ($F = 2.67$) falls short of the critical value; the interaction ($F = 24.00$) and maze ($F = 42.67$) are well beyond it.
:::

And what that means is that there was a significant difference between the two maze conditions overall. Kids took longer on the hard maze, in general, than on the easy maze. But there was no difference between the two audience conditions in general. On average, kids didn't do any better or worse being watched than working alone. But we have a significant interaction, and a significant interaction means that the main effects don't mean too much by themselves, because the interaction tells us that the effect of one factor depends on the level of the other.

<!-- PLAN (2026-11-11): "Visualizing the results" moved from here to "Reporting results", with the graphs (fig-maze-results). A forward pointer might be wanted here. -->

### Step 5: Estimate the effect and follow up

#### Effect size: partial $\eta^2$

<!-- FIX (2026-11-09): Chapter 15's reason for the partial version (conditions could never explain differences between people) doesn't carry over to a second manipulated factor, so it needs its own reason here. The three values add up to more than 1 (.78 + .18 + .67), which clashes with the bucket picture unless it's explained. Each denominator below is also just that effect's $SS$ plus $SS_{\text{within}}$, which would match the form used in Chapter 15. -->

<!-- FIX: "when we get significant results" conflicts with Chapter 14 (always report effect size). The worked equations label these $\eta^2_A$ etc., while the prose and report call them $\eta^2_p$. -->

To complete our hypothesis test, when we get significant results, we need to quantify the effect size. Here, as for other ANOVAs, we use eta squared. Like the related samples ANOVA, we're actually using partial eta squared, one for each of our tests. There's the effect size for the main effect of Factor A, another effect size for Factor B, and another for the interaction, just like we have three $F$ ratios.

In each case, the numerator is the $SS$ for that component of the variability and the denominator is the partial variability, excluding the other sources that we quantify separately. So the partial $\eta^2$ for the main effect of Factor A is the $SS$ for Factor A divided by the total $SS$ minus the $SS$ for Factor B and for the interaction. We're partialling out those other sources of variability that we quantify separately. For Factor B, it's $SS_B$ over $SS_{\text{total}}$ minus $SS_A$ and $SS_{\text{interaction}}$. And for the interaction, it's the $SS$ for the interaction over $SS_{\text{total}}$ minus $SS_A$ and $SS_B$.

$$
\begin{align}
\eta^2_A &= \frac{SS_A}{SS_{\text{total}} - SS_B - SS_{A \times B}} = \frac{1{,}024}{1{,}952 - 64 - 576} = 0.78 \\
\eta^2_B &= \frac{SS_B}{SS_{\text{total}} - SS_A - SS_{A \times B}} = \frac{64}{1{,}952 - 1{,}024 - 576} = 0.18 \\
\eta^2_{A \times B} &= \frac{SS_{A \times B}}{SS_{\text{total}} - SS_A - SS_B} = \frac{576}{1{,}952 - 1{,}024 - 64} = 0.67
\end{align}
$$

#### Simple effects

Test the effect of one factor at each level of the other, using $MS_{\text{within}}$. For these data: on the easy maze, watched kids were 8 seconds faster, $F(1, 12) = 5.33$, $p = .040$; on the hard maze, 16 seconds slower, $F(1, 12) = 21.33$, $p < .001$. ## Reporting and interpreting results

### Reporting results

And lastly, we report the results. As always, this is a fairly dry, technical statement. For the descriptives, meaning the means for each condition, there are so many to report here that it can get messy doing it in a sentence, so a table or a graph is usually preferred. And you need to mention the type of test you performed, including here specifying what each of the factors was and what the dependent variable — the thing you measured and are comparing — was. And you need to report the test results with $F$ ratios, degrees of freedom, and $p$ value for each of the three tests, including effect size for any significant tests.

<!-- FIX (2026-11-09): names and numbers swapped into the old report. The last clause now describes the pattern in the cell means, which needs the simple effects to back it up. Still to bring into line with Chapters 14 and 15: exact $p$ values (audience $p = .128$; maze and interaction $p < .001$), an effect size for every test (audience $\eta^2_p = .18$), and the descriptives. -->

> To examine the influence of maze difficulty and an audience on performance, a 2-factor ANOVA was conducted with completion times as the dependent variable and Maze Difficulty and Audience as between-participants independent variables. There was no significant main effect of Audience ($F(1, 12) = 2.67$, $p > .05$). There was, however, a significant main effect of Maze Difficulty ($F(1, 12) = 42.67$, $p < .05$, $\eta^2_p = .78$); overall, times were longer on the hard maze. Moreover, there was a significant interaction between Maze Difficulty and Audience ($F(1, 12) = 24.00$, $p < .05$, $\eta^2_p = .67$); being watched went with faster times on the easy maze but slower times on the hard maze.

<!-- PLAN (2026-11-12, Rob): graphing *these* results is part of reporting them, so it's two static figures here. Reading *other* possible patterns is the tutorial in "Interpreting the results". The two paragraphs around the figure came from Step 4's "Visualizing the results" and the old graph section; the first one's cross-reference now points at the figure. Check the joins, and whether they sit better before the written report than after it. "Lower times are faster" may still need saying.
     DRAFT (gap) for the second graph, which is new: same four means, audience on the x-axis. The easy line falls from 36 to 28 and the hard line rises from 40 to 56, so the lines don't cross here, though they do in the first graph. Nothing about the data changed, only which factor we put on the axis. Crossing is one way of being non-parallel; not parallel is what shows an interaction. -->

<!-- FIX (2026-11-09): the second sentence was about the banana's main effect; it now makes the matching point about audience, which has no significant main effect, so the logic runs the other way round. Check it. -->

This is what I meant by the interaction quantifying patterns of cell means that deviate from what you'd expect based on the main effects. The lack of a main effect of audience suggests that being watched doesn't generally matter. But the interaction tells us it isn't quite so simple. Visualizing the results in a line graph, as in @fig-maze-results, shows the trends more clearly.

::::

Each dot represents one of the four group means. The x-axis has the two levels of one factor and the levels of the other factor are represented by different lines, joining up the dots by the levels of that factor. For kids working alone, represented by the solid line, there was barely any difference between the easy maze and the hard maze. But that wasn't the case for kids being watched. For them, represented by the dashed line, the hard maze took much longer than the easy one. Put another way, it looks like being watched made kids faster on the easy maze and slower on the hard maze.

### Interpreting the results

<!-- CUT (2026-11-11; the generic Factor A / Factor B walk-through that went with the four static graphs, replaced by the "What if?" steps above). Kept verbatim, minus the figures and quizzes.

### No main effect of A, main effect of B, no interaction

So here's a basic generic version of a two-by-two line graph. Again, Factor A is represented as groups on the x-axis and Factor B is represented as the different lines joining up the dots, which represent each of the four group means. But for this example, we just have two lines and they're both parallel to the x-axis.

Let's think through how to interpret this basic pattern of findings. Think about the main effects first. Is there a main effect of Factor A? If there was, we would see that in the slope of the lines. If scores generally increased or decreased between the two levels of Factor A, the lines would slant up or down. Here they're completely flat, which is what we'd see with no main effect of Factor A — no difference in how people scored in level one of Factor A as compared to level two of Factor A overall. Is there a main effect of Factor B? We would see that in the distance between the lines. Here there's a big gap. Scores were generally higher in level two of Factor B as compared to level one of Factor B. So that indicates a main effect of Factor B. The interaction is evident in whether or not the lines are parallel. Here they are. This means that the main effect of Factor A is the same at all levels of Factor B and vice versa.

So again, here there is no main effect of Factor A. There is a main effect of Factor B — level two scores are higher than level one scores overall. And that is equally true at both levels of Factor A. That's what we mean by not having an interaction.

### Main effects of both A and B, no interaction

Here's another example. Now the lines slope up to the right.

So see if you think there are significant main effects of Factor A, Factor B, and an interaction.

Again, here, the slope of the line suggests that there is a main effect of Factor A — scores are higher across the board in level two of Factor A than in level one. And like the previous graph, there is still a wide gap between the lines, suggesting a main effect of Factor B — scores are generally higher in level two of Factor B than level one. But there's still no interaction. The lines are parallel, meaning that the main effect of A is the same at both levels of Factor B and vice versa.

### Crossover interaction

None of those previous examples showed an interaction. This is what an interaction might look like. Again, the interaction is revealed by lines which are not parallel to one another. This is called a crossover interaction because, as you can see, the lines cross over. And this is where interpreting the findings gets a little trickier.

Here there would be no main effect of Factor A because the average score for level one and level two would be about the same. Likewise, there would be no main effect of Factor B because, again, the average scores would be about the same between the two levels of Factor B. But the lack of main effects clearly doesn't tell the whole story, because there is this interesting crossover interaction going on.

For level one of Factor A, scores are higher if you were in level two of Factor B than level one. But in level two of Factor A, the pattern was reversed. Scores were higher in level one of Factor B than in level two.

### Another interaction example

Here's another example of an interaction.

Here Factor A had no effect on people in level one of Factor B, but it did have an effect on people in level two of Factor B. It's important that you understand how to read these kinds of graphs and interpret the overall pattern of results from a factorial ANOVA.
-->

## Practice: Design your own example

Again, it's a complicated thing. And maybe it doesn't help that much talking about it in such abstract terms, since Factor A and Factor B don't intuitively mean anything. So I'd like you to come up with an example of your own, or to describe a study you've learned about somewhere else that fits this two-by-two design. It should be a design with two independent variables, each with two levels, and one dependent variable — the measure for which scores are recorded and compared across groups. Anytime I'm thinking about this kind of design, I literally just sketch a little graph like the ones earlier in this chapter with four dots, one for each group's average score — just whether I think it's going to be relatively high or low or in the middle — and then join up the dots to represent the levels of the factors.
